Patient Vignette: Mr. A.

Mr. A. is a 76-year-old widower who presents to the clinic at the urging of his daughter. He works part-time as a cashier at a local hardware store, a job he took five years ago after his wife passed away, primarily to have a reason to leave the house. He is a thin, slightly stooped man who speaks in a quiet, deliberate manner, often pausing to look down at his hands before answering a question.

The story he tells begins not in the present, but in the winter of 1944, when he was a small boy in a city under siege. He describes the sound first—a low, droning hum that would grow into a terrible shriek. He remembers his mother’s hand, cold and bony, gripping his as they ran for the cellar. The cellar was always damp, smelling of earth and coal dust and fear. He remembers the way the candle flame would jump when a bomb landed close, and the way the grown-ups would press their fingers to their lips, shushing the children who cried. He was six years old. He learned to be silent.

That winter, his family’s apartment building took a direct hit. He was not home; he was at a neighbor’s. He remembers the strange, sucking silence after the blast, and then the dust. He walked home through a world turned gray and jagged. He found his mother standing in the street, her coat torn, her face a mask of white powder. She was holding a piece of their front door. She did not look at him. She just said, “Your father is gone.” He never saw his father’s body. He never knew where he was buried.

Now, seventy years later, Mr. A. lives in a quiet suburban neighborhood. He keeps his windows closed, even in summer. He explains, with a small, apologetic smile, that the sound of a garbage truck backing up—that beeping—makes his heart feel like it will “jump out of his chest.” He avoids the hardware store’s loading dock. When a customer drops a box of nails or a heavy wrench clatters to the linoleum floor, he feels a jolt go through him, a sudden hot flash that leaves his hands trembling. He has to steady himself on the counter. He tells his manager it’s a “bad back.”

He has trouble sleeping. He lies in bed, rigid, listening. He listens for the drone, for the shriek that never comes. The silence of his own house feels charged, like the air before a storm. He often wakes up on the floor, having rolled out of bed in his sleep, his body curled into a tight ball. He does not remember having a nightmare, only the feeling of a great weight pressing down on him.

The worst part, he says, is the feeling of being watched. Not by a person, but by the past. It is a pressure behind his eyes, a sense that the gray, dusty world of 1944 is just a thin veil away. He sometimes catches a whiff of damp earth and coal dust in his own clean living room. He will be ringing up a customer’s purchase—a bag of birdseed, a new hammer—and for a split second, the face in front of him will blur, replaced by the memory of a neighbor’s terrified expression. He blinks, and it is gone.

He avoids the television news. The images of other wars, other ruined cities, feel like a personal violation. He cannot watch a movie with explosions. He says he feels “foolish” for being so affected, so long after. He was just a child. He was not a soldier. “I didn’t do anything,” he says, his voice barely a whisper. “I just hid.”

His daughter says he has become a ghost. He is present, but he is not there. He spends his days off sitting in his armchair, staring at the wall. He has stopped going to the senior center. The noise, the chatter, the sudden laughter—it all feels too unpredictable. He tells his daughter he is just tired. But he is not tired. He is waiting. He is six years old again, holding his breath in the dark, waiting for the all-clear that never seems to come.
